```{r setup}
library(energyRt)
```

```{r feature-flags, include = FALSE}
# Sections of this article describe work that lands in stages. Each flag turns
# its section's chunks on as the feature arrives, so the article never shows a
# result the installed version cannot produce.
has_bridge      <- exists("convert_path")
has_currency    <- exists("currency_fx")
has_model_units <- "units" %in% methods::slotNames("config")
# the slot being there is not the conversion being there, and neither is the
# data: the normaliser is its own feature
has_currency_norm <- exists("normalize_model_currency")

# Where a feature is not in the running build, say so above its examples --
# otherwise the code renders with no output and reads as if it should work.
.not_yet <- function(flag, what) {
  if (isTRUE(flag)) return(invisible(NULL))
  cat(sprintf(paste0(
    "\n> **Not in this build.** %s is not available in energyRt %s. ",
    "The calls below are shown for reference; their output will appear here ",
    "once the feature lands.\n\n"),
    what, as.character(utils::packageVersion("energyRt"))))
}
```

A model is arithmetic on numbers whose meaning lives outside the numbers. A coal
plant costing `2000` is meaningless until you know whether that is EUR per kW or
MEUR per GW, and whether the coal it burns is counted in PJ or in tonnes. This
article covers where each unit is declared, how `convert()` moves between them,
and what the model checks for you.

# Where units live

One slot carries units, and its columns name what is being measured.

| Where | Column | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| Commodity, or a flow | `@units$comm` | in what measure is this commodity counted? |
| Process | `@units$capacity`, `$activity`, `$use` | what are this process's capacity and activity units? |
| Anything priced | `@units$currency` | what money are its costs in? |
| Weather | `@units$wval` | what does the series measure, if anything? |
| Model | `config@units` | what should everything be expressed in? |

A commodity's `@units$comm` is its **native measure** — the one the model
balances it in. Electricity in GWh, coal in PJ, water in Mm3. The `unit =`
argument of a constructor writes it, and `getUnit()` reads it back:

```{r comm-unit}
ELC <- newCommodity("ELC", desc = "Electricity", unit = "GWh")
COA <- newCommodity("COA", desc = "Steam coal",  unit = "PJ")
getUnit(COA)
```

A process declares its own units in `@units`, which is where a cost currency is
stated:

```{r tech-units}
EGAS <- newTechnology(
  name = "EGAS", desc = "Gas turbine",
  input  = data.frame(comm = "GAS", unit = "PJ"),
  output = data.frame(comm = "ELC", unit = "GWh"),
  units  = data.frame(capacity = "GW", activity = "GWh", currency = "MEUR"),
  invcost = data.frame(invcost = 0.9),         # MEUR per GW
  varom   = data.frame(varom = 0.003),         # MEUR per GWh
  cap2act = 8760)                              # 1 GW × 8760 h = 8760 GWh
```

`getUnits()` shows what an object declares and what each of its parameters is
therefore measured in. It composes the answer from the slots above and the
dimensional meaning of each parameter — investment cost is *costs per capacity*,
variable cost is *costs per activity*, and so on:

```{r get-units}
getUnits(EGAS)
```

Where a process leaves a unit undeclared, `getUnits()` shows the placeholder
token (`{costs}`, `{capacity}`, `{activity}`) rather than guessing.

Up to version 0.91 a commodity's and a flow's own measure was a slot of its
own, `@unit`, beside the `@units` table a process carried. The two are one
slot now, so `getUnit()` and `getUnits()` read the same place. `unit =` is
still the constructor argument, which is why the code above is unchanged, and
a saved object's `@unit` is migrated to `@units$comm` when it is read.

# Dimensions and conversion

Every unit belongs to a **dimension** — energy, mass, volume, time, currency and
so on. Two units are interconvertible when they share one, and `convert()` is
the function that does it:

```{r convert-basic}
convert("PJ", "GWh")        # 1 PJ is how many GWh?
convert("kWh", "MJ")
convert("toe", "GJ")
```

The third argument is the value to convert, so a whole column can go through at
once:

```{r convert-value}
convert("EUR/kW", "MEUR/GW", 2000)     # capex catalogue value -> model units
convert("MMBtu", "MWh", c(1, 10, 100))
```

Compound units are built from `/`, `*` and `^`, and SI prefixes attach to the
symbols that accept them. Note that `EUR/kW` and `MEUR/GW` are the *same* unit —
the mega on top cancels the giga underneath — which is why the call above
returns its input unchanged and is worth writing anyway: it documents the
catalogue's units in the code.

## What deliberately will not convert

Some things are refused rather than guessed at, and the refusals are deliberate.

**Different dimensions do not convert.** `convert("t", "PJ")` has no answer
without knowing *what substance* is being weighed — that is the subject of the
next section.

**`MBtu` is not accepted.** In oil and gas `M` is the Roman thousand, so `MBtu`
means 1000 Btu; under SI it would mean 1e6 Btu. The two readings differ by a
factor of 1000, so `Btu` does not take SI prefixes at all and `MMBtu` must be
written out. Write `MMBtu`, or `kJ`/`GJ` if you want prefixes that behave.

**Spellings are case-sensitive.** `mW` is a milliwatt and `MW` is a megawatt, a
factor of 1e9 apart, so there is no case-insensitive fallback anywhere in the
unit system. `BTU` is not `Btu`.

# Physical properties: crossing dimensions

A tonne of coal and a petajoule of coal are the same coal. Moving between them
needs a physical fact — a heating value — and that fact belongs to the
commodity. `commodity@property` is where it lives:

```{r comm-property}
COA <- newCommodity(
  "COA", desc = "Steam coal", unit = "PJ",
  property = data.frame(
    property = c("lhv", "hhv", "density", "frac_C"),
    value    = c(25.8,  27.1,  0.85,      0.665),
    unit     = c("GJ/t", "GJ/t", "t/m3",  "kg/kg"),
    comment  = c("IEA average, other bituminous", "",
                 "bulk, as stockpiled", "ultimate analysis")))

commodity_property(COA, "lhv")
```

The recognised property names, and the dimension pair each one relates, are in
`commodity_properties()`:

```{r comm-properties-registry}
commodity_properties()[, c("property", "quantity", "default_unit")]
```

The key idea is that **a property whose unit is a ratio of two dimensions is a
conversion factor between them**. `lhv = 25.8 GJ/t` is an energy-to-mass edge;
`density = 0.85 t/m3` is a mass-to-volume edge. Chain them and a volume of coal
becomes an energy. Given the properties, `convert()` can find that chain itself:

```{r not-yet-bridge, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
.not_yet(has_bridge, "Commodity-aware conversion")
```

```{r convert-commodity, eval = has_bridge}
convert(1, "t",  "GJ", commodity = COA)   # 25.8   — via lhv
convert(1, "m3", "GJ", commodity = COA)   # 21.93  — via density, then lhv
convert(1, COA, "Mt")                     # 0.03876 — COA's native PJ into Mt
convert_path("m3", "GJ", commodity = COA) # which properties it used
```

Because a commodity can stand wherever a unit string can, two commodities can be
compared directly — but only once you say **what is being held constant**:

```{r convert-comm-to-comm, eval = has_bridge}
convert(1, COA, ELC, "energy")   # 1 PJ of coal as GWh of electricity
```

That fourth argument is not decoration. Coal and electricity are not physically
interconvertible; the only thing that can carry across is a shared dimension,
and which one is a modelling choice rather than a fact. Where the choice is
unambiguous it is inferred, and where it is not `convert()` reports the
candidates and the number each would give rather than picking one.

## When a property is ambiguous

Some commodities have more than one value for what looks like one property.
Hydrogen has three densities, spanning nearly three orders of magnitude:

```{r h2-property}
H2 <- newCommodity(
  "H2", desc = "Hydrogen", unit = "PJ",
  property = data.frame(
    property = c("lhv", "hhv", "density", "density_liquid", "density_700bar",
                 "molar_mass"),
    value    = c(120.0, 141.8, 8.988e-5, 0.07085, 0.0420, 2.016),
    unit     = c("GJ/t", "GJ/t", "t/m3", "t/m3", "t/m3", "g/mol"),
    comment  = c("119.96 MJ/kg", "141.88 MJ/kg", "gas, 0 C, 1 atm",
                 "liquid, -253 C", "compressed, 700 bar", "")))
```

Only the bare name joins the default set of conversion edges, so `density` — the
one the model works in — is used unless you name a variant. The same holds for
`lhv` against `hhv`:

```{r h2-convert, eval = has_bridge}
convert(1, "m3", "MJ", commodity = H2)                          # 10.79, NTP gas
convert(1, "m3", "MJ", commodity = H2, via = "density_liquid")  # 8502
convert(1, "t",  "GJ", commodity = H2, via = "hhv")             # 141.8
```

The first two differ by a factor of 788, which is exactly why the state has to be
named rather than assumed.

::: {.callout-note}
**A property describes the commodity itself.** Anything whose numerator is a
*different* commodity — a CO2 emission factor, say — belongs in `@emis`, which
is what the model actually reads. The two stay consistent: coal's carbon
fraction times 44.009/12.011, divided by its heating value, reproduces the
per-energy emission factor, which makes `@emis` checkable rather than
duplicated.
:::

# Money is a unit with a year

Currency is a dimension like any other, so `convert("MEUR", "MUSD")` works. But
money has a property no physical unit has: **it changes value over time**. A cost
of 1000 EUR is not one number, it is one number and a year.

Write the year into the unit:

```{r not-yet-currency, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
.not_yet(has_currency, "Year-tagged currency")
```

```{r currency-tagged, eval = has_currency}
convert(1, "MEUR2020", "MUSD2020")   # an exchange-rate question
convert(1, "MUSD2015", "MUSD2020")   # an inflation question
```

Those are two different problems and they need two different kinds of data:
**exchange rates** move between currencies at one point in time, **deflators**
move between points in time within one currency.

|            | 2015 | → | 2020 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EUR**    | `MEUR2015` | *deflator (euro)* | `MEUR2020` |
| ↓          | *FX 2015*  |  | *FX 2020* |
| **USD**    | `MUSD2015` | *deflator (US)* | `MUSD2020` |

An exchange rate belongs to a currency, but a deflator belongs to an economy,
and a currency need not be one: there is no euro-area deflator in these
series, so the euro deflates on its largest member. Which economy stood in is
recorded rather than implied — that is what `currency_deflator$area` is for.

Read that table as a square. To get from the top-left to the bottom-right you
can go along and then down, or down and then along — and **the two routes do not
give the same answer**. That is not a defect in the arithmetic: the gap between
them *is* the change in the real exchange rate over the interval, and it is zero
only if purchasing power parity held.

```{r currency-spread, include = FALSE, eval = has_currency}
# Measured against the shipped tables rather than typed into the prose: these
# are properties of the data, and an earlier draft of this article quoted
# numbers that the tables, once they existed, did not support.
.spread <- function(a, b) {
  r <- suppressWarnings(convert(1, a, b, currency_route = "both"))
  max(r) / min(r)
}
.eur <- .spread("MEUR2015", "MUSD2020")
.jpy <- .spread("MJPY2012", "MUSD2023")
```

How far apart they are is a question for the data. Between 2015 and 2020 the
euro and the dollar part company by
`r if (has_currency) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (.eur - 1)) else "a few percent"`;
between 2012 and 2023 the yen and the dollar differ by a factor of
`r if (has_currency) sprintf("%.2f", .jpy) else "about two"` — the yen lost
half its dollar value over an interval in which Japanese prices barely moved,
which is a large change in the real exchange rate and so a large gap between
the routes.

So both are always computed. The default follows the World Bank and IPCC
convention — deflate in the source currency, then convert at the target year —
and you are warned when the routes disagree materially:

```{r currency-route, eval = has_currency}
convert(1, "MJPY2012", "MUSD2023")                              # default route
convert(1, "MJPY2012", "MUSD2023", currency_route = "both")     # see both
```

Both tables are annual, cover every currency the series carry, and are built
by `data-raw/currency.R` from a cached pull that ships with the sources, so a
number in a result can be traced to the row it came from and the whole table
can be rebuilt. They stop at the year they were built from; a rate newer than
the release, or one of your own, goes in for the session:

```{r currency-add, eval = has_currency}
add_currency_fx("EUR", 2026, 0.92, source = "my own estimate")
convert(1, "MEUR2026", "MUSD2026")
```

**Untagged money consults no deflator.** A conversion where neither side
carries a year is a pure exchange rate, read at the one year
`attr(currency_fx, "base_year")` names, and it never warns. What did change in
this release is where that rate comes from: the coefficients used to be typed
in by hand and undated — they carried a euro rate from one year beside a yen
rate from another — and they are now generated from the annual series at a
single stated year. So untagged cross-currency answers moved once, here, and a
conversion within one currency (`convert("EUR/kW", "MEUR/GW")`, a prefix ratio)
did not move at all.

```{r currency-untagged, eval = has_currency}
convert("EUR/kW", "MEUR/GW")        # a prefix ratio: no rate is consulted
attr(currency_fx, "base_year")      # the year untagged money is read at
currency_base_year(2020)            # or pin it somewhere else
convert("MEUR", "MUSD")
currency_base_year(attr(currency_fx, "base_year"))
```

# What the model enforces

A model has exactly one currency whether it says so or not: the objective adds
every cost together with coefficient 1, across regions as well as processes. So
declare it, in the same slot and under the same column name an object uses:

```{r not-yet-model-units, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
.not_yet(has_model_units, "A model-level unit target")
```

```{r model-units, eval = has_model_units}
mod <- newModel("demo", units = data.frame(currency = "MUSD"))
mod@config@units$currency
```

`currency =` is the shorter way to write the same thing, and what every example
before this release used: `newModel("demo", currency = "MUSD")`. It was the
`config@currency` slot up to version 0.91.

What this enforces is that the pair can be **reconciled**. An object that
declares a currency must declare one the model's can be reached from; one that
declares nothing is in the model's own currency, which is what a model-level
declaration means. The check runs at `newModel()`, so a declaration that leads
nowhere is refused where it was written rather than surfacing in a model much
later:

```{r model-currency-check, error = TRUE}
COAL <- newSupply("COAL", commodity = "COA", unit = "PJ",
                  units = data.frame(currency = "bnEUR"))
newModel("demo", currency = "MUSD", data = add(newRepository("r"), COAL))
```

A mismatch that *can* be converted is not an error, it is work. Where an
object was priced in another currency-year, its costs are converted to the
model's and every factor applied is reported — never applied silently:

```{r not-yet-norm, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
.not_yet(has_currency_norm, "Currency normalisation")
```

```{r currency-norm, eval = has_currency_norm, message = TRUE}
PV <- newTechnology("PV", units = data.frame(capacity = "GW",
                                             currency = "MEUR2015"),
                    invcost = data.frame(invcost = 700))
GAS_SUP <- newSupply("GAS_SUP", commodity = "GAS", unit = "PJ",
                     units = data.frame(currency = "MUSD2015"),
                     supply = data.frame(cost = 8))
mod <- newModel("demo", currency = "MUSD2020",
                data = add(newRepository("r"), newCommodity("GAS"), PV,
                           GAS_SUP))
mod <- normalize_model_currency(mod)
```

The factors are the article's two questions, one each: `PV` crosses a currency
and a year, `GAS_SUP` crosses only a year and so moves on the US deflator alone,
where the route cannot matter. Every one is recorded, with the exchange-rate
and deflator rows behind it, so a result can be traced back to its inputs:

```{r currency-norm-report, eval = has_currency_norm}
mod@misc$currency$objects
mod@misc$currency$deflator
```

`interpolate_model()` does this on the copy it builds from, where the report
lands in `scen@misc$currency`. Objects are therefore left as you wrote them:
`getData()` on a process returns the values you authored, while `getData()` on
the scenario returns the normalised ones.

Two things this does **not** do, stated plainly so you do not assume
otherwise. Physical units are not normalised — a technology declaring its coal
input in Mt while the commodity is PJ is not corrected, only conversion helpers
know how to relate them. And normalising to a constant currency-year commits
`wacc` and `sdr` to being **real** rates; nothing checks that the rate you
supplied is real rather than nominal.
